title: 2 Kings 17:1–6
context: Hoshea, Israel’s last king, becomes a vassal of Assyria, then withholds tribute and seeks help from Egypt. The Assyrian king imprisons him, besieges Samaria for three years, and deports Israel. The synchronism with Ahaz in 17:1 is one of several chronological difficulties in this period (compare 15:30; 18:1, 9-10), and Assyrian records raise the question of whether Shalmaneser or his successor Sargon completed the capture; interpreters reconstruct these details in different ways.

verses.text: In the twelfth year of Ahaz king of Judah, Hoshea the son of Elah began to reign in Samaria over Israel for nine years.
verses.arminianNotes: Hoshea begins a nine-year reign as Israel’s last king. Arminian readers note that even at the end, each king still faced a real choice about whom to trust, and Hoshea’s reign shows how late that opportunity extended.
verses.reformedNotes: The synchronism with Ahaz is difficult to align with 15:30 and 18:1, 9-10, and interpreters offer several reconstructions. Reformed readers treat these as genuine questions while affirming that the narrative’s theological meaning does not depend on resolving them.

verses.text: He did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, yet not as the kings of Israel who were before him.
verses.arminianNotes: Hoshea did evil, though not as the kings before him. Arminian readers note that Scripture recognizes degrees of faithfulness, and that a less wicked king was still accountable for not returning wholeheartedly to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that judgment falls in the reign of a king who was not the worst. The exile is the outcome of generations of sin, not the failure of one man alone, as 17:7-23 explains.

verses.text: Shalmaneser king of Assyria came up against him; and Hoshea became his servant, and brought him tribute.
verses.arminianNotes: Shalmaneser comes against Hoshea, who becomes his servant and pays tribute. Arminian readers see the political pressures of the age, in which survival seemed to depend on submitting to the strongest empire.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Assyria’s rise serves God’s purposes of judgment, a theme Isaiah develops when he calls Assyria the rod of God’s anger (Isaiah 10:5). The king is called Shalmaneser here, and Assyrian records name his successor in connection with Samaria’s fall.

verses.text: The king of Assyria discovered a conspiracy in Hoshea; for he had sent messengers to So king of Egypt, and offered no tribute to the king of Assyria, as he had done year by year. Therefore the king of Assyria seized him, and bound him in prison.
verses.arminianNotes: Hoshea conspires with So king of Egypt and stops paying tribute. Arminian readers see a desperate gamble that relied on another earthly power instead of returning to the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: The identity of So is uncertain; some suggest a pharaoh of the period, others a place name, and no proposal is settled. Reformed readers see the futility of trusting Egypt, a theme the prophets repeat (compare Hosea 7:11).

verses.text: Then the king of Assyria came up throughout all the land, went up to Samaria, and besieged it three years.
verses.arminianNotes: The Assyrian king invades the land and besieges Samaria for three years. Arminian readers note the length of the siege, which allowed time for repentance even as judgment closed in.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the siege as the outworking of covenant curses warned of long before (Deuteronomy 28:49-52). The capital Omri built now endures the siege the law had threatened.

verses.text: In the ninth year of Hoshea the king of Assyria took Samaria and carried Israel away to Assyria, and placed them in Halah, and on the Habor, the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes.
verses.arminianNotes: In Hoshea’s ninth year Samaria falls, and Israel is deported to Halah, the Habor, Gozan, and the cities of the Medes. Arminian readers feel the weight of a people uprooted from the land God had given them.
verses.reformedNotes: The places named are generally located in upper Mesopotamia and the Iranian plateau, though precise sites are debated. Reformed readers see the exile as the scattering threatened in Deuteronomy 28:64, fulfilled after long patience.
